thesis: Decision quality must be judged with prior information, not merely outcome.

ideas.statement: Luck and skill coexist; compare methods across equivalent tasks.
Preserve falsifiability and the agency to revise or leave.

evidenceAndExamples.statement: Dana defends her failed attack: “It was a good decision.” Her friend, who won without a plan, replies: “The outcome says otherwise.” This is a fictional dispute, but its dilemma is precise. What are we judging: the decision made before the outcome, or the outcome we already know?

In a world without uncertainty, the difference would be smaller. If we knew every consequence perfectly, a good choice could be evaluated directly by those consequences. In mixed games, as in many real situations, we must judge a choice on the information available at the time, not with the retrospective advantage of knowing what happened.

In Risk, troop numbers and the rules for rolling dice change the probability of conquest. Mathematical analyses such as that by Hendel and colleagues calculate these relationships. The existence of dice does not mean all attacks are equally rational. It means a decision can change the distribution of outcomes without determining the individual outcome. [46]

Suppose, purely as an example, there are two options with the same gain and the same loss. The first has a 70% chance of success, the second 30%. Choosing the first is justified under these simplified conditions. If we lose, it does not follow that the probabilities have reversed. If we choose the second and win, we have not demonstrated some mysterious competence.

In real life, the assumptions of the example are rarely so clean. Sometimes we do not know the probabilities; sometimes we care about avoiding a catastrophic loss rather than maximizing the average. That is precisely why the verdict “it worked, so it was good” is insufficient.

A generated program can pass the public demonstration and fail in production. A hypothesis can seem confirmed in a small sample and collapse under a new test. Confusing luck with merit requires no psychopathology. Failing to keep a record of the original criteria is enough.

Potter van Loon, van den Assem, and van Dolder analyzed approximately 76.9 million hands of online poker. The persistence of relative performance supports the existence of a skill component. It does not follow that a skilled player wins every hand or that experience guarantees profit. The study shows why the simple opposition between “luck” and “intelligence” poorly describes certain activities. [4]

The lesson for an LLM user is surprisingly similar. A well-formulated request can receive a poor answer. A vague request can accidentally produce something excellent. If we learn only from the immediate impression, we may adopt useless rituals and abandon useful practices.

A user might come to believe that a particular compliment to the model unlocks a secret capability, simply because a good solution appeared afterward. To find out whether the wording really helps, it must be compared across several equivalent tasks, rather than venerating the moment when it worked.

There is a seductive hypothesis: we might also appreciate chance because it distributes explanations conveniently. A win can be attributed to skill, a defeat to bad luck. We will not treat this as a proven explanation of a preference for all games. It is a question about how we tell our own story.

The LLM adds a lawyer available around the clock. It can be invited to explain why failure does not refute the idea, why the test was unsuitable, or why the critics did not understand. Some of these defenses may be correct. A test can be poor; a critic can be wrong. The problem begins when no imaginable observation can count against us anymore.
Then we no longer have a strategy encountering chance. We have a story protected against every outcome.

Chess reminds us that surprise does not require explicit randomness. People can fascinate one another through choices, depth, and the limits of calculation. In a novel, the ending is already written, but the reader does not yet know it. An open future can be a property of our experience rather than of the universe itself.

This observation protects us from a technological mistake. We need not artificially introduce unpredictability into every tool to make it interesting. A system that responds consistently, shows what it knows, and discovers new constraints with us can support compelling exploration.

Agency does not necessarily mean the power to control every outcome. It can mean the power to formulate the question, change strategy, recognize an error, or leave the table. The last of these powers will become one of the most important in this book.

objectionsAndQualifications.statement: Probabilities in real settings may be unknown and catastrophic risks matter.

audit.notes: Complete chapter read; preserve proposed concepts, empirical limits and non-diagnostic distinctions.
